lead: A throttling calorimeter measures steam dryness without collecting water. Wet steam at pressure p₁ passes through a throttle to a lower pressure p₂ and leaves superheated. The steady flow energy equation, with no work, little heat loss and small kinetic and potential energy changes, gives h₁ = h₂. The steam tables turn the outlet p₂ and T₂ into h₂, and with h<sub>f</sub> and h<sub>fg</sub> at the inlet pressure p₁ that gives the dryness x₁. Boiler trials and steam laboratories use it to check the steam sent to engines and turbines. Steam calorimetry belongs to steam laboratory work.
prereq: You need dryness fraction, the steam tables, and the steady flow energy equation from the first law for open systems.

blocks.text: Wet steam at p₁ enters a throttle, a small orifice or valve. It leaves at lower p₂. The process is throttling: no work, negligible heat transfer, small kinetic and potential energy changes. The steady flow energy equation gives h₁ = h₂. h₁ is inlet specific enthalpy, kJ/kg; h₂ is outlet specific enthalpy, kJ/kg.

blocks.where: h<sub>f1</sub> is saturated liquid enthalpy at inlet pressure p₁, kJ/kg; h<sub>fg1</sub> is latent heat at p₁, kJ/kg; x₁ is inlet dryness fraction.

blocks.text: To use this, the outlet must be superheated. Then p₂ and T₂ fix h₂ in the superheated table. At inlet, h₁ = h<sub>f1</sub> + x₁ h<sub>fg1</sub>. Substituting h₁ = h₂ gives the formula above.

items: Read inlet pressure p₁, outlet pressure p₂ and outlet temperature T₂.
Confirm the outlet is superheated at p₂ and T₂.
Find h₂ from the superheated steam table.
Find h<sub>f1</sub> and h<sub>fg1</sub> at p₁ from the saturated steam table.

blocks.text: If the outlet is still wet, h₂ depends on an unknown outlet dryness x₂. The equation h₁ = h₂ then has two unknowns, so the throttling calorimeter is invalid. The limit is easy to compute. With p₂ = 1 bar the outlet is just dry when h₂ = h<sub>g</sub> = 2675.0 kJ/kg, so at p₁ = 10 bar the wettest steam the instrument can read is x₁ = (2675.0 − 762.5)/2014.6 = 0.949. Steam wetter than about 95 per cent needs the separating calorimeter.

A separating calorimeter works mechanically. Steam passes through baffles that turn it sharply; water droplets hit the walls and drain into a measuring vessel. The steam that leaves is nearly dry; it is condensed and weighed. Let m<sub>w</sub> be the separated water mass and m<sub>s</sub> the mass of steam that passed, over the same time. Then x<sub>s</sub> = m<sub>s</sub>/(m<sub>s</sub> + m<sub>w</sub>).

This instrument suits very wet steam, but it is less exact: some fine droplets pass with the steam, so x<sub>s</sub> overstates the dryness. A combined separating and throttling calorimeter first removes most of the water; the throttling part then measures the dryness x<sub>t</sub> of the steam that passed. The dryness of the main steam is x = x<sub>s</sub> × x<sub>t</sub>.

items: Throttling calorimeter: outlet must be superheated; needs accurate p₁, p₂ and T₂.
Separating calorimeter: direct mass measurement; used when steam is very wet.
Combined unit: separating part handles bulk water, throttling part gives fine dryness.
Both need steady flow and a representative steam sample.

examples.question: Wet steam at 10 bar is throttled to 1 bar and 130 °C. At 10 bar, h<sub>f</sub> = 762.5 kJ/kg and h<sub>fg</sub> = 2014.6 kJ/kg. At 1 bar and 130 °C, h = 2736.7 kJ/kg. Find the inlet dryness fraction x₁.
steps: Check the outlet state: at 1 bar the saturation temperature is 99.6 °C, so 130 °C is superheated by about 30 K.
Read the outlet enthalpy from the superheated table: h₂ = 2736.7 kJ/kg.
At the inlet pressure 10 bar: h<sub>f1</sub> = 762.5 kJ/kg and h<sub>fg1</sub> = 2014.6 kJ/kg.
Check: 0.980 is above the limit 0.949 found for 10 bar, so the outlet can indeed be superheated.
examples.answer: x₁ ≈ 0.980, so the steam is 98.0 per cent dry.

examples.question: In a combined test on the same 10 bar main, the separator collects 0.5 kg of water while 9.5 kg of steam passes on to the throttling part, which gives the outlet state of the first example (1 bar, 130 °C). Find the dryness fraction of the main steam.
steps: Throttling part: x<sub>t</sub> = 0.980, as in the first example.
Vapour in the sample: x<sub>t</sub> × m<sub>s</sub> = 0.980 × 9.5 = 9.31 kg, out of a total of 9.5 + 0.5 = 10 kg.
x = 9.31/10 = 0.931, which is the same as x<sub>s</sub> × x<sub>t</sub> = 0.95 × 0.980.
examples.answer: The main steam has x ≈ 0.931, too wet for the throttling calorimeter alone (limit 0.949 at 10 bar).

traps: Using h₁ = h₂ when the outlet is still wet. Then h₂ contains unknown x₂ and the calculation cannot give x₁.
Forgetting to check that the outlet is superheated. A temperature alone does not fix h₂ inside the wet region.
Taking h<sub>f</sub> and h<sub>fg</sub> at the outlet pressure. Both must be at the inlet pressure p₁.
Swapping h<sub>f</sub> and h<sub>fg</sub> in x₁ = (h₂ − h<sub>f1</sub>)/h<sub>fg1</sub>. h<sub>fg1</sub> is the latent heat, not the sensible part.
Applying h₁ = h₂ with large kinetic or potential energy changes. The throttle must be well insulated and changes small.

quiz.q: State the enthalpy relation used by a throttling calorimeter.
quiz.a: For steady throttling with no work, little heat loss and small kinetic and potential energy changes, h₁ = h₂.

quiz.q: Why must the outlet of a throttling calorimeter be superheated?
quiz.a: Only then do p₂ and T₂ fix h₂ from the superheated table. If the outlet is wet, h₂ also depends on an unknown x₂.

quiz.q: Wet steam at 10 bar (h<sub>f</sub> = 762.5 kJ/kg, h<sub>fg</sub> = 2014.6 kJ/kg) is throttled to 1 bar and 120 °C, where h = 2716.6 kJ/kg. Find x₁.
A throttling calorimeter test gives an outlet that is still wet. What should you conclude?
quiz.a: The test is invalid for finding x₁. Use a separating calorimeter or a combined separating and throttling calorimeter.

quiz.q: Write the dryness fraction from a separating calorimeter in terms of masses.
quiz.a: x = m<sub>s</sub>/(m<sub>s</sub> + m<sub>w</sub>), where m<sub>s</sub> is dry steam mass and m<sub>w</sub> is separated water mass.

quiz.q: Why is a separating calorimeter preferred for very wet steam?
quiz.a: Very wet steam may not become superheated after throttling, so the throttling calorimeter fails. The separating calorimeter removes water and measures masses directly.

quiz.q: Steam at 5 bar (h<sub>f</sub> = 640.1 kJ/kg, h<sub>fg</sub> = 2108.0 kJ/kg) is throttled to 1 bar (h<sub>g</sub> = 2675.0 kJ/kg). What is the lowest dryness this calorimeter can read?
quiz.a: The outlet is just dry when h₂ = 2675.0 kJ/kg, so x<sub>min</sub> = (2675.0 − 640.1)/2108.0 = 2034.9/2108.0 = 0.965. Wetter steam leaves the throttle still wet.

beyond: Not for the exam. Power plants use continuous steam-quality instruments based on throttling, separation or light scattering. Combined separating and throttling calorimeters appear in older laboratory manuals and in some boiler test codes. Newer work uses acoustic and optical methods for wet-steam measurement. Search for 'throttling calorimeter', 'separating calorimeter' and 'steam quality measurement'.
